Commitment: Lower inflation and grow the economy to ease the cost of living and create better paying jobs.
Notes: Annual inflation at 3.1% in March 2026 (down from 7.3% peak), still above RBNZ 1-3% target. Economy avoiding recession but 'rocky' (Westpac May 2026); real wages growing but cost-of-living remains a concern. Tax relief delivered but broader growth weak.

Commitment: Let Kiwis keep more of what they earn with tax relief of up to $100 per fortnight for an average income household and a FamilyBoost childcare tax credit of up to $150 per fortnight.
Build infrastructure with 13 new Roads of National Significant and four major public transport upgrades.
Notes: Initial action: "Begin work on a new GPS reflecting the new Roads of National Significance and new public transport priorities." Oct 2025: NZTA Board endorsed investment cases for all RoNS; $675m+ in funding for design/consenting and $515m for property acquisition approved. Construction already underway on Takitimu North Link Stage 1, SH29 Tauriko West, and Otaki to north of Levin. Progress on 15 RoNS rather than original 13.

Commitment: Restore law and order by backing Police to tackle gangs, boot camps for serious young offenders, and stronger sentencing so New Zealanders can feel safe
Notes: Gang legislation in force: 76 patches and 315 insignia seized by Feb 2025. Two Oranga Tamariki boot camps run (2024 pilot, second from Mar 2026), though 7/10 reoffended. Three Strikes restored. Government reports violent crime reduction target tracking ahead (Aug 2025); Feb 2026 figures show drop in victim numbers. Mixed outcomes on boot camps.

Commitment: Lift school achievement by teaching kids an hour each of reading, writing and maths every day, banning cell phone use at school, and regular assessment and reporting to parents.
Cut health waiting times by training more doctors, nurses, and midwives, and giving Kiwis access to 13 more cancer treatments.
Support seniors by maintaining the Winter Energy Payment, increasing Super every year and boosting it with our tax relief plan, which will see a superannuitant couple get over $600 extra each year.
Notes: Winter Energy Payment maintained; NZ Super indexed annually. Tax relief component ($100/fortnight, FamilyBoost) delivered (see row 3). Researchers and Greens now calling to replace WEP with solar subsidy, but WEP still in place as of June 2026.

Commitment: Deliver Net Zero by 2050 including by doubling New Zealand’s renewable electricity and supporting new technology to reduce agricultural emissions.
Notes: Dec 2024: Second Emissions Reduction Plan released. Aug 2024: Electrify NZ plan with RMA reforms for renewables. Dec 2025: Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill introduced. $2bn BlackRock fund for 100% renewable electricity. More renewable generation commissioned in past 18 months than 15 years. BUT: Government axed Clean Car Discount, weakened methane pricing, and ETS reform; ag emissions policy ambiguous.

Commitment: Tax relief will be progressed as set out in National’s Tax Plan, but will not include a repeal of the foreign buyer’s residential property ban, with income tax reductions coming into force from 1 July 2024
Reduce Core Crown expenditure as a proportion of the overall economy.
Establish a select committee inquiry into banking competition with broad and deep criteria to focus on competitiveness, customer services, and profitability.
Explore options to strengthen the powers of the Grocery Commissioner, to improve competitiveness, and to address the lack of a third entrant to remove the market power of a duopoly
Notes: Grocery Industry Competition Act now law; Commissioner actively enforcing (warned Woolworths Jan 2026, taken Foodstuffs North Island to court). Aug 2025 'express lane' for new supermarkets; Woolworths exiting NZ. Mar 2026: Government backed away from 'nuclear option' of breaking up duopoly. Foodstuffs and Woolworths still 82% of market - no third entrant achieved.

Commitment: Assess and respond to the impact that energy prices have on inflation including consumer led institutional improvements.
Notes: Some retailers offering 'hour of free power' (Sept 2025); Commerce Commission making anonymous reporting tool for businesses on electricity companies (Aug 2025); Parliament debated power costs Oct 2025. OCR held at 2.25% by RBNZ May 2026. No major institutional reform delivered; calls to renationalise power market rejected by major parties.

Commitment: By or before 2026, assess the impact inflation has had on the average tax rates faced by income earners.
As an export dependent nation, prioritise free and fair trade agreements, including with India
Notes: India FTA signed in New Delhi 28 April 2026. Coalition parties publicly disagreed over what was signed up; Labour backed the deal. NZ has also signed FTAs with UAE, UK, and EU during the term.

Commitment: The Coalition Government will increase funding for IRD tax audits to urgently expand the IRD tax audit capacity, minimise taxation losses due to insufficient IRD oversight, and to ensure greater integrity and fairness in our tax system
Notes: IRD enforcement intensity increased (Jul 2025 'cracks down' warning) but no specific evidence of increased funding for tax audit capacity. Commitment to expanded IRD audit capacity appears largely undelivered as a budget measure.

Commitment: Strengthen obligations on Jobseeker work ready beneficiaries to find work and make use of sanctions for non-compliance with work obligations, and consider time limits for under 25s.
Commit to moderate increases to the minimum wage every year.
Notes: Minimum wage reached $23.95/hr by Apr 2026 (up from $20 in 2021). Annual increases have been delivered - though Labour/Greens called Apr 2026 increase 'measly' (below inflation). Sustained moderate increases throughout the term.

Commitment: Improve the Accredited Employer Work Visa to focus the immigration system on attracting the workers and skills New Zealand needs.
Notes: Active AEWV reform programme: English requirements expanded (changes from 1 Jun 2026); Minister Stanford got tough on employers choosing migrants over locals (Oct 2025); migrant bus drivers need post-graduate English for residency (Sept 2025). Reforms ongoing and substantial.

Commitment: Ensure Immigration New Zealand is engaged in proper risk management and verification to ensure migrants are filling genuine workforce needs.
Notes: INZ strengthened law enforcement tools Apr 2024 with infringement penalties. Auditor-General Nov 2024 said visa systems need sharper focus. Exploitation cases continue (Kiwifruit boss fined $40k May 2026, Thai massage business fined, dairy farmer fined $200k). Some action but significant gaps remain.

Commitment: Investigate the establishment of an “Essential Worker” workforce planning mechanism to better plan for skill or labour shortages in the long term.
Commit to enforcement and action to ensure those found responsible for the abuse of migrant workers face appropriate consequences.
Notes: Jun 2026: Budget 2026 sets aside $18m over 4 years for migrant exploitation enforcement. Jul 2025: Bill criminalising migrant exploitation (up to 7 years jail, $100k fines). Apr 2024: INZ infringement penalties in effect. Multiple successful prosecutions: Kiwifruit boss $40k, Thai massage $200k+, dairy farmer $200k.

Commitment: Address and provide solutions for the long-expressed concern of the OECD into the lack of focus in New Zealand Immigration Policy
Notes: May 2024 OECD report flagged immigration alongside inflation, education, productivity. Government has substantially reshaped immigration settings (AEWV reforms, English requirements, parent visa threshold hikes, Skilled Migrant changes). OECD's 'lack of focus' critique partially addressed by broad migration reset.

Commitment: Establish a National Infrastructure Agency
Notes: Jun 2026: 30-year National Infrastructure Plan released and backed by Parliament with cross-party support (Labour and Greens). New Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport starts 1 Jul 2026 (Bishop defending it 19 Jun 2026). Original commitment was a 'National Infrastructure Agency'; actual delivery is a different structure but achieves similar function.

Commitment: Prioritise strategic infrastructure to improve the resilience of heavy industry in New Zealand.
Notes: May 2026: NZ First (Peters) proposed Special Economic Zone at Marsden Point. Dec 2025: RMA replacement bills include infrastructure resilience provisions. No specific heavy industry resilience programme delivered; commitment remains largely unaddressed.

Commitment: Establish a Regional Infrastructure Fund with $1.2 billion in capital funding over the Parliamentary term.
Repeal the Natural and Built Environment Act 2023 and the Spatial Planning Act 2023.
Amend the Resource Management Act 1991
Notes: Dec 2025: RMA shakeup passed under urgency; Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill introduced to replace RMA. Apr 2025: 'Reforming the reforms' debate. Multiple RMA Amendment Bills (1st, 2nd, 3rd) progressing through Parliament. RMA replacement aim is passage in 2026. Substantial progress but full replacement not yet law.

Commitment: Cancel Auckland Light Rail
Cancel Let's Get Wellington Moving
Reduce expenditure on cycleways
Commit to building a four-lane highway alternative for the Brynderwyns and investigate the use of private finance to accelerate construction.
Notes: Route selection for the new Northland Expressway over the Brynderwyn Hills was announced in April 2025, with the replacement road to be built just east of the current SH1 alignment.

Commitment: Investigate the threshold at which local lines companies can invest in generation assets.
Commission a study into New Zealand’s fuel security requirements.
Facilitate the development and efficiency of ports and strengthen international supply networks.
Commence an urgent review into the implementation of the National Policy Statement on Indigenous Biodiversity before any implementation.
Replace the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020 and the National Environmental Standards for Freshwater to better reflect the interests of all water users.

Investigate the reopening of Marsden Point Refinery. This includes establishing a Fuel Security Plan to safeguard our transport and logistics systems and emergency services from any international or domestic disruption.
Notes: Strategic diesel reserve at Marsden Point officially operational 7 July 2026 (two refurbished tanks
column14: managed by Z Energy) — Fuel Security Plan limb delivered; refinery itself not reopening.

Commitment: Progress further work examining connecting the railway to Marsden Point and Northport from the Northern Main Truck Line.

Progress the detailed business case for a dry dock at Marsden Point to service domestic and international shipping needs and to support our Navy vessels, with investigation of funding options including commercial partnerships.
Notes: A Marsden Point dry dock has been identified as likely candidate for Northland's $1.2b Regional Infrastructure Fund wish list (Sept 2024), with detailed business case work to follow.

Commitment: Require the electricity regulator to implement regulations such that there is sufficient electricity infrastructure to ensure security of supply and avoid excessive prices.
Notes: Transpower was given additional powers to manage electricity supply risks in March 2025 as the sector sought to avoid a repeat of the prior year's shortages.

Commitment: Examine transmission and connection pricing to facilitate cost effective connection of new renewable generation resources, both on-shore and off-shore.
Plan for transitional low carbon fuels, including the infrastructure needed to increase the use of methanol and hydrogen to achieve sovereign fuel resilience.
Notes: Simeon Brown announced in June 2026 an LNG import terminal is being progressed as part of sovereign fuel resilience, with steeper fines for non-compliant power companies.

Commitment: Future-proof the natural gas industry by restarting offshore exploration and supporting development of hydrogen technology to produce hydrogen from natural gas without co-production of CO2.
Notes: Offshore petroleum exploration ban lifted in Sept 2024; in Jan 2026 EnZed Energy's application to explore a south Taranaki block became the first offshore bid under consideration since the reversal.

Commitment: Ensure that climate change policies are aligned and do not undermine national energy security.
Ensure the government’s energy settings allow for the exploration of natural geological hydrogen in New Zealand, to maximise future energy resilience.
Investigate the strategic opportunities in New Zealand’s mineral resources, including vanadium, and develop a plan to develop these opportunities.
Notes: Government released a list of 35 critical minerals in Sept 2024 as part of Shane Jones' mineral mining strategy, with vanadium explicitly identified; sector strategy targets doubling mineral exports to $2b by 2035. 6 Jul 2026: Govt committed up to $50m from the Regional Infrastructure Fund to Tāiko Critical Minerals (Barrytown) and Westland Mineral Sands (Westport) processing projects — strategy moving from planning into funded delivery.

Commitment: Stop the current review of the ETS system to restore confidence and certainty to the carbon trading market.
Notes: Government exempted farmers from ETS pricing in June 2024 and set up a new working group, effectively halting the prior He Waka Eke Noa pricing workstream.

Commitment: Progress work to recognise other forms of carbon sequestration, including blue carbon.
Notes: Nov 2025: Government identified new wetlands and rewetted peatlands as areas of opportunity for carbon removal, expanding recognition of sequestration beyond forestry.

Commitment: Incentivise the uptake of emissions reduction mitigations, such as low methane genetics, and low methane producing animal feed.
Notes: Related agricultural emissions mitigation work continues via the new working group established June 2024, though no specific scheme for low-methane genetics/feed yet announced.

Commitment: Support Farm Environment Plans administered by regional councils and targeted at a catchment level.
Adopt standardised farm level reporting.
Cut red tape and regulatory blocks on irrigation, water storage, managed aquifer recharge and flood protection schemes.
Amend the National Environmental Standards for Plantation Forestry (NES-PF) regulations to place a duty upon harvesters to contain and remove post-harvest slash.
Direct government agencies where practical and appropriate to preference the use of woollen fibres rather than artificial fibres in government buildings.
Notes: April 2025: New government procurement rules direct agencies to prefer wool over synthetic fibres; Kāinga Ora subsequently committed to woollen carpet in new state homes (June 2025).

Commitment: Reverse the recent ban on live animal exports while ensuring the highest standards of animal welfare.
Notes: Government U-turned in March 2026, announcing live animal exports will NOT resume this term — a binary deliverable explicitly abandoned.

Commitment: Reform the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee to ensure its functions, membership and mandate are appropriate.
Notes: Oct 2025: Associate Agriculture Minister overrode NAWAC concerns to rewrite pig welfare rules, demonstrating restructuring of NAWAC's effective mandate.

Commitment: Deliver longer durations for marine farming permits and remove regulations that impede the productivity and enormous potential of the seafood sector.
Liberalise genetic engineering laws while ensuring strong protections for human health and the environment.
Notes: Select Committee has considered the Gene Technology Bill but stalled ahead of second reading; NZ First said in June 2026 the overhaul is unlikely before the election.

Commitment: Commit to training no fewer than 500 new frontline police within the first two years.
Increase the number of the trained Youth Aid Officers over the term.
Notes: No specific Youth Aid Officer numbers reported. Adjacent action: Government announced new community police teams in major cities (June 2024), but Youth Aid Officer data not surfaced.

Commitment: Adequately resource community policing, including Māori and Pasifika wardens, Community Patrol New Zealand, and Neighbourhood Watch.
Notes: First public action: community police teams announced in major cities (June 2024); national gang unit established (May 2024). No specific ringfenced funding boost for Māori/Pasifika wardens, Community Patrol NZ or Neighbourhood Watch found.

Commitment: Introduce a suite of measures designed to tackle youth crime including consideration of a Youth Justice Demerit Point system.
Reform the Fleeing Driver laws to curb the increase in fleeing driver incidents.
Notes: Antisocial Road Use Legislation Amendment Bill passed final reading 30 June 2026 — presumptive vehicle forfeiture for fleeing drivers/street racers, new Police powers to close roads at antisocial gatherings, infringement fees for excessive vehicle noise lifted $50→$300. Most changes in force in six months.

Commitment: Amend the Sentencing Act 2002 and associated legislation to ensure appropriate consequences for criminals, including: Giving priority to the needs of victims and communities over offenders. Including gang membership as an aggravating factor during sentencing. Including the victim working sole charge or adjacent to a dwelling as an aggravating factor during sentencing. Ensuring real consequences for lower-level crimes such as shoplifting. Removing concurrent sentences for those who commit offences while on parole, on bail, or whilst in custody.
Notes: Strong progress: gang membership as aggravating sentencing factor passed Sept 2024; three-strikes reinstated Dec 2024; concurrent sentencing for parole/bail/custody offences and shoplifting instant fines (Jul 2025). 'Real consequences for lower-level crimes' largely delivered.

Commitment: Where appropriate, require prisoners to work, including in the construction of new accommodation in prisons or pest control.
Notes: No specific prisoner-work programme rollout found beyond the youth boot camp pilot (Palmerston North, Jul 2024–2025). General prison labour programmes predate the commitment.

Commitment: Equip corrections officers with body cameras and protective equipment, where appropriate.
Notes: RNZ explainer (9 Sep 2025) confirms NZ Police still don't routinely wear body cameras; corrections officer rollout not separately documented. Some prison site trials exist but no broad deployment.

Commitment: Seek to make it easier for New Zealanders, including prisoners, to get drivers licences, and better support to existing programmes that are delivering positive outcomes.
Notes: Whangārei community court tackling unlicensed driving launched Aug 2024 (adjacent). No specific 'easier licensing for prisoners' programme identified.

Commitment: Introduce the Protection for First Responders and Prison Officers legislation which will create a specific offence for assaults on first responders which includes minimum mandatory prison sentences.
Notes: Justice Minister Goldsmith announced specific offence for assaulting first responders (29–30 Jun 2025). Status reflects announcement stage; passage not yet confirmed by available sources.

Commitment: Introduce the Coward Punch legislation which will create a specific offence for anyone who injures or kills someone with a coward punch.
Notes: Coward Punch offences (8 yrs GBH / 15 yrs intended GBH / life for culpable homicide) announced 30 Jun 2025. NZ First publicly labelled the enacted law 'window dressing' on 12 Jun 2026 — committed but seen as weaker than promised.

Commitment: Investigate the introduction and implementation of Degrees of Murder Sentencing legislation.
Enforce compulsory education and address truancy.
Refocus the curriculum on academic achievement and not ideology, including the removal and replacement of the gender, sexuality, and relationship-based education guidelines.
Notes: Old guidelines removed from Ministry of Education website Feb 2025. Government began consulting on new draft relationships & sexuality education framework 15 Apr 2025. Curriculum refocus ongoing under Stanford.

Commitment: Stop first year Fees Free and replace with a final year Fees Free with no change before 2025.
Notes: First-year Fees Free stopped and final-year scheme launched 1 Jan 2025 as planned, but Peters/Willis confirmed scrapping of final-year Fees Free in the 2026 Budget (8 May 2026) — partial implementation then walked back.

Commitment: Maintain the Apprenticeship Boost scheme.
Notes: No explicit announcement found maintaining or expanding Apprenticeship Boost under the coalition — implicit continuation through TEC contracts. Treat as low-confidence positive fraction.

Commitment: Abolish the Māori Health Authority.
Update Pharmac’s decision making model to ensure it appropriately takes “patient’s voice” into account and increase funding for Pharmac every year.
Notes: Pharmac funding increased $604m June 2024. Patient-voice progress: new working group established Jul 2025; Patient Voice Aotearoa report Apr 2026 criticised slow decision-making. Decision-making model not yet formally reformed.

Commitment: Require Medsafe to approve new pharmaceuticals within 30 days of them being approved by at least two overseas regulatory agencies recognised by New Zealand.
Notes: Medicines Amendment Bill (parallel assessment) at Select Committee 5 Jun 2025 — incremental progress beyond Q3 action plan.

Commitment: Better recognise people with overseas medical qualifications and experience for accreditation in New Zealand.
Notes: Medical Council fast-tracked specialist registration from Nov 2024 and GP applications from US/Canada/Singapore from Jul 2025. 70% of new doctor registrations are now overseas-trained.

Commitment: Progress the adoption of digital technology in harder to staff areas and make greater use of Nurse Practitioners.
Notes: Budget 2026 allocated $153.6m for Health NZ digital/cyber upgrades (29 May 2026). No specific Nurse Practitioner scope-of-practice expansion surfaced.

Commitment: Repeal the Therapeutic Products Act 2023.
Fund Gumboot Friday/I Am Hope Charity to $6 million per annum.
Renegotiate the Crown funding agreement with St John with a view to meeting a greater portion of their annualised budget.
Notes: Budget 2026 included $35m for ambulance services — two new Auckland hubs, more staff, technology upgrades (22 May 2026). Partial progress on renegotiated Crown funding agreement.

Commitment: Ensure Plunket is funded to do their job properly.
Ensure proper funding for birthing units and maternity care, including providing for a three day stay for new mothers.
Notes: Government committed to a Bill enabling 3-day postnatal stay (11 Oct 2025), but PM Luxon clarified on 2 Jun 2026 that prior social-media framing was 'incorrectly characterised'. Birthing-unit funding situation unclear.

Commitment: Repeal amendments to the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act 1990 and regulations before March 2024, removing requirements for denicotisation, removing the reduction in retail outlets and the generation ban, while also amending vaping product requirements and taxing smoked products only.
Notes: Smokefree amendments repealed in 100-day plan (denicotisation, retail reduction, generation ban removed); further Smokefree/Vaping changes pushed through under urgency 13 Dec 2024. Smoking-only taxation less clear.

Commitment: Reform the regulation of vaping, smokeless tobacco and oral nicotine products while banning disposable vaping products and increasing penalties for illegal sales to those under 18.
Notes: Disposable vapes banned from 16 Jun 2025; stricter advertising rules in force; increased penalties for illegal sales. Comprehensive reform package largely delivered.

Commitment: Keep the superannuation age at 65.
Notes: Superannuation eligibility age maintained at 65. Coalition KiwiSaver discussion (Jun 2026) is separate from super age.

Commitment: Amend the Building Act and the Resource Consent system to make it easier to build granny flats or other small structures up to 60sqm requiring only an engineer’s report.
Notes: Government announced policy to allow buildings up to 60sqm without resource consent in certain areas (5 Apr 2025). Building Act amendment progressing — partial delivery, engineer-only regime not yet finalised.

Commitment: Progress the review of the Retirement Villages Act.
Notes: Retirement Villages Amendment Bill now exists: residents paid interest after 6 months of leaving a unit, full repayment guaranteed within 12 months (announced Jun 2026). Coalition 'review' has produced a legislative vehicle, though residents and Labour consider 12 months inadequate. Not yet enacted.

Commitment: Upgrade the Super Gold Card and Veterans Card to maximise its potential benefit for all Super Gold Card and Veteran Card holders.
Investigate the funding formula for new residential care beds.
Notes: 17 Jun 2026: $79m (~4%) funding boost for aged residential care for 2026/27
column12: tied to ministerial advisory group work that Costello said will report in the next few weeks. First concrete funding formula response; full reform recommendations still pending.

Commitment: Engage openly and constructively with the aged-care sector.
Notes: Government has engaged with the aged-care sector via a ministerial advisory group with sector 'liaison' on nominees, but no formal engagement framework has been published.

Commitment: Undertake a select committee inquiry into aged care provision to include supporting people with early onset conditions and what asset thresholds are appropriate in 2023/24.
Notes: A select committee inquiry into aged care provision has been completed; it is explicitly cited as informing the 2025 ministerial advisory group work.

Commitment: Explore options to build on the Local Government Rates Rebate Scheme for Super Gold Card holders.
Work on establishing bipartisan agreement to fund both care and dementia beds that New Zealand needs now and with a focus on the long term needs by 2040.
Liaise with retirement village owners and occupiers to seek a mutually agreed way forward to safeguard the interests of the 50,000 plus New Zealanders living in retirement villages.
Notes: Government's Retirement Villages Amendment Bill (6-month interest, 12-month repayment guarantee) shows the 'mutually agreed' engagement has produced legislative change — though residents (and Labour) consider the 12-month timeframe inadequate. Bill not yet enacted.

Commitment: By December 1, 2023, lodge a reservation against adopting amendments to WHO health regulations to allow the government to consider these against a “national interest test”.
References: Confirmed by email from NZ First.

Commitment: Commit that in the absence of a referendum, our Government will not change the official name of New Zealand.
Support to select committee a bill that would enact a binding referendum on a four-year term of parliament.
Notes: See "Constitution (Enabling a 4-Year Term) Amendment Bill" commitment from ACT. Constitution (Enabling a 4-Year Term) Amendment Bill was debated at first reading in March 2025; select committee recommended a referendum in August 2025.

Commitment: Ensure publicly funded sporting bodies support fair competition that is not compromised by rules relating to gender.
Notes: Government ordered Sport NZ to scrap and remove trans-inclusive community sport guidelines in July 2025; IOC also brought in new gender eligibility rules in March 2026, aligning NZ policy direction.

Commitment: Legislate to make English an official language of New Zealand.
Notes: English Language Bill introduced February 2026, first reading passed, currently before select committee with report due 3 September 2026.

Commitment: Ensure all public service departments have their primary name in English, except for those specifically related to Māori.
Notes: 20 May 2026: Public Service Commission directive from Minister Goldsmith required all agencies to update websites by end of June 2026 with 'New Zealand Government' in bold above 'Te Kāwanatanga o Aotearoa'. Coalition agreement milestone achieved via central directive; physical materials to follow.

Commitment: Require the public service departments and Crown Entities to communicate primarily in English - except those entities specifically related to Māori.
Notes: Partial implementation via individual agency directives (Health NZ, NZTA) but no comprehensive English-first communication directive across all departments; te reo rollback continues piecemeal.

Commitment: Protect freedom of speech by ruling out the introduction of hate speech legislation and stop the Law Commission’s work on hate speech legislation.
Notes: Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith ordered the Law Commission to stop hate speech work in April 2024 and confirmed no new hate speech legislation will proceed; both halves of the commitment delivered.

Commitment: End all Covid-19 vaccine mandates still in operation.
Notes: Some workplace madnates are still in effect as of May 2024 All remaining legal Covid-19 vaccine mandates were already scrapped in August 2023 before the coalition took office; by May 2024 the government acknowledged there was nothing left to end.

Commitment: Ensure, as a matter of urgency in establishment and completion, a full scale, wide ranging, independent inquiry conducted publicly with local and international experts, into how the Covid pandemic was handled in New Zealand, including covering: use of multiple lockdowns, vaccine procurement and efficacy, the social and economic impacts on both regional and national levels, and whether the decisions made, and steps taken, where justified.

Ensure a ‘National Interest Test’ is undertaken before New Zealand accepts any agreements from the UN and its agencies that limit national decision-making and reconfirm that New Zealand’s domestic law holds primacy over any international agreements.

The Coalition Government will defend the principle that New Zealanders are equal before the law, with the same rights and obligations, and with the guarantee of the privileges and responsibilities of equal citizenship in New Zealand.
Notes: Cabinet Office circular on need-not-race (Sept 2024) and ongoing Treaty Principles / equal-citizenship messaging provide an initial basis, but no dedicated 'equal before the law' legislation.

Commitment: The Coalition Government will work to improve outcomes for all New Zealanders, and will not advance policies that seek to ascribe different rights and responsibilities to New Zealanders on the basis of their race or ancestry.
Notes: Government's Sept 2024 need-not-race Cabinet circular is a first-step directive; broader race-based rights reform has been pursued via Treaty Principles Bill (defeated April 2025).

Commitment: The Coalition Government will honour the undertakings made by the Crown through past Treaty of Waitangi settlements.
Remove co-governance from the delivery of public services.
Notes: Co-governance has been partially unwound (Māori Health Authority abolished, school Treaty duties removed, English-first agency names) but the headline Treaty Principles Bill was defeated 11-112 in April 2025; commitment has not been fully delivered.

Commitment: Restore the right to local referendum on the establishment or ongoing use of Māori wards, including requiring a referendum on any wards established without referendum at the next Local Body elections.
Stop all work on He Puapua
Confirm that the Coalition Government does not recognise the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) as having any binding legal effect on New Zealand.
Notes: Government has not formally affirmed UNDRIP domestically and Māori leaders have raised NZ's UN review in 2025; no positive statement binding on NZ has been issued.

Commitment: Amend section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area Act to make clear Parliament’s original intent, in light of the judgment of the Court of Appeal in Whakatohea Kotahitanga Waka (Edwards) & Ors v Te Kahui and Whakatohea Maori Trust Board & Ors [2023] NZCA 504.
Notes: Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill was introduced Sept 2024, paused after Dec 2024 Supreme Court ruling, then reactivated August 2025 to override the 2023 Court of Appeal decision.

Commitment: Amend the Waitangi Tribunal legislation to refocus the scope, purpose, and nature of its inquiries back to the original intent of that legislation.

Conduct a comprehensive review of all legislation (except when it is related to, orsubstantive to, existing full and final Treaty settlements) that includes “The Principles ofthe Treaty of Waitangi” and replace all such references with specific words relating to therelevance and application of the Treaty, or repeal the references.
The Government will not progress the development and delivery of National’s manifesto commitment to a “Taxpayer’s Receipt” for taxpayers.

National’s Going for Housing Growth policy will now accommodate the ACT/National agreement to make the Medium Density Residential Standards (MDRS) optional for councils, and to consider sharing a portion of GST collected on new residential builds with councils.
Notes: Government's major RMA reform unveiled Dec 2025 — two replacement bills (Planning Act, Natural Environment Act) introduced and bridge Duration of Consents bill passed under urgency. MDRS optionality addressed in replacement architecture but takes effect 2029.

Commitment: The Parties confirm no ongoing commitment to income tax changes, including threshold adjustments, beyond those to be delivered in 2024.
Notes: Negative commitment honored: no further income tax threshold adjustments delivered beyond 2024 tax package across Budgets 2024, 2025 and 2026. Coalition pledge to refrain from further income tax changes appears to have been kept.

Commitment: Full cost benefit analysis must be presented before any binding agreement is made with respect to the Waikato medical school.
Notes: Initial action: Sign an MoU with Waikato University to progress a third medical school.

Commitment: National’s commitment to supercharge electric vehicle infrastructure with a comprehensive, nationwide network of 10,000 public EV chargers by 2030 will specifically take into account ACT’s concern that there be robust cost benefit analysis to ensure maximum benefit for government investment.
Notes: Public EV charging network programme continues; no major milestone found in 2025-26 but the 2024 beehive release sets the foundation. Status defensible as continuing rollout.

Commitment: Legislate to improve the quality of regulation, ensuring that regulatory decisions are based on principles of good law-making and economic efficiency, by passing the Regulatory Standards Act as soon as practicable.
Notes: Regulatory Standards Bill progressed to select committee by Jul 2025, with officials warning of $60m/yr cost. Bill remains in legislative pipeline; not yet enacted.

Commitment: Immediately establish a new ministerial portfolio for Regulation.

Establish a new government department, required to assess the quality of new and existing legislation and regulation, funded by disestablishing the Productivity Commission and consolidating some regulatory quality work across the public sector where appropriate.

In consultation with the relevant Minister, carry out regulation sector reviews, which could include the primary industries, the finance sector, early childhood education, and healthcare occupational licencing, in each case producing an omnibus bill for regulatory reform of laws affecting the sector.
Rewrite the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act 2003 to protect vulnerable consumers without unnecessarily limiting access to credit.
Amend the Overseas Investment Act 2005 to limit ministerial decision making to national security concerns and make such decision making more timely.
Notes: Initial action: Take policy decisions to amend the Overseas Investment Act 2005 to make it easier for build-to-rent housing to be developed in New Zealand.

Commitment: Reform market studies introduced by the Commerce Amendment Act 2018 to focus on reducing regulatory barriers to new entrants to drive competition.

Deliver savings in public sector spending by reducing non-essential back office functions, with expenditure reduction targets to be set for each agency, informed by the increase in back office head count at that agency since 2017.
Notes: Budget 2024 delivered 240 back-office savings initiatives including corporate services cuts at Police, FMA, Archives NZ, Government Property Group, etc.; ongoing back-office efficiency work in subsequent budgets.

Commitment: Restore mortgage interest deductibility for rental properties with a 60 per cent deduction in 2023/24, 80 per cent in 2024/25, and 100 per cent in 2025/26.
Notes: 80% deduction from 1 April 2024, 100% from April 2025 implemented. The 60% backdated deduction for 2023/24 was abandoned ('not worth the benefit' — Seymour). 2 of 3 schedule steps delivered.

Commitment: Repeal the Clean Car Discount.
Narrow the Reserve Bank’s remit, to focus on price stability, and take advice on replacing “medium term” with specific time targets.
Amend the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 2021 to remove the dual mandate and take advice on removing the Treasury observer and returning to a single decision maker model
Notes: Dual mandate removed via RBNZ (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill, passed under urgency Dec 2023. Treasury observer removal and single decision maker model — no public progress found.

Commitment: Repeal the Fair Pay Agreement regime by Christmas 2023.
Reform health and safety law and regulations.
Expand 90-day trials to apply to all businesses.

Consider simplifying personal grievances and in particular removing the eligibility for remedies if the employee is at fault, and setting an income threshold above which a personal grievance could not bepursued.
Maintain the status quo that contractors who have explicitly signed up for a contracting arrangement can’t challenge their employment status in the Employment Court.
Increase the cap on the number of workers under the Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme to increase the flexibility of the quota allocation system.
Introduce a five year, renewable parent category visa, conditional on covering healthcare costs, with consideration of a public healthcare levy.
Notes: Parent Boost visa announced 10 June 2025; applications opened 29 September 2025. Multi-entry 5-year visa, renewable once (up to 10 years total). ACT's Parmjeet Parmar confirmed commitment fulfilled. Healthcare levy replaced with private health insurance requirement — substantive deviation from ACT's original proposal.

Commitment: Remove median wage requirements from Skilled Migrant Category visas.
Notes: SMC reforms announced; median wage requirement for residence removed as part of two new residency pathways (skilled work experience, trades/technician) taking effect late August 2026. New red/amber occupation lists add complexity.

Commitment: Liberalise the rules to make it easier for family members of visa holders to work in New Zealand, beginning with Skilled Migrant Category visa holders.
Notes: Initial action: government expanding work rights for international students (Mar 2026) and revamping open work visa conditions — partial movement on liberalising family member work rights, but specific Skilled Migrant Category family work reforms not yet legislated.

Commitment: Amend the Resource Management Act 1991 to make it easier to consent new infrastructure including: renewable energy, allow farmers to farm, get more houses built, and enable aquaculture and otherprimary industries.
Notes: Multiple RMA bills progressed: first amendment May 2024, several more in 2025, plus Resource Management (Duration of Consents) Amendment Bill passed under urgency Dec 2025. Major RMA replacement bills introduced Dec 2025.

Commitment: Replace the Resource Management Act 1991 with new resource management laws premised on the enjoyment of property rights as a guiding principle.
Notes: Two replacement Acts (Planning Act, Natural Environment Act) introduced Dec 2025; premised on property rights per Bishop/Court. Not scheduled to take effect until 2029, with select committee in 2026.

Commitment: Institute long-term city and regional infrastructure deals, allowing PPPs, tolling and value capture rating to fund infrastructure.
Notes: Initial action: Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop publicly flagged congestion charges, road tolls, water metres, and PPPs as the funding path. No enabling legislation enacted yet — first public articulation of the toolkit.

Commitment: Introduce financial incentives for councils to enable more housing, including considering sharing a portion of GST collected on new residential builds with councils.
Notes: Partial: government has used resource consenting reforms and other mechanisms to incentivise council housing growth, but specific GST-sharing mechanism with councils for new residential builds has not been legislated.

Commitment: Legislate to make the MDRS optional for councils, with the need for councils to ratify any use of MDRS, including existing zones.
Remove the Kāinga Ora Sustaining Tenancies Framework and ensure appropriate consequences for tenants who engage in repeated antisocial behaviour.
Notes: March 2024 letter from housing and finance ministers directed Kāinga Ora to replace the Sustaining Tenancies Framework; by 1 June 2025, 63 Kāinga Ora tenancies had been terminated in the resulting behaviour crackdown (600% increase in formal warnings).

Commitment: Explore allowing home builders to opt out of needing a building consent provided they have long-term insurance for the building work.
Work to replace fuel excise taxes with electronic road user charging for all vehicles, starting with electric vehicles.
Work with Auckland Council to implement time of use road charging to reduce congestion and improve travel time reliability.
Notes: Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Bill passed third reading 11 November 2025, establishing framework permitting local authorities to set up congestion charging by notifying NZTA. Auckland CBD scheme still to be implemented.

Commitment: Reverse speed limit reductions where it is safe to do so.
Allow landlords to issue a 90 day notice to a tenant to end a periodic tenancy without providing a reason or applying to the Tenancy Tribunal.
Return tenants’ notice period to 21 days and landlords’ to 42 if the tenant wished to move or landlord wished to sell a property.
Introduce “pet bonds” to make it easier for tenants to have pets in rental properties.

Maintain a split-gas approach to methane and carbon dioxide through to 2050 and review the methane science and targets in 2024 for consistency with no additional warming from agricultural methane emissions.
Notes: Independent panel reviewed 2050 methane target April 2024; government confirmed split-gas approach in October 2025 by lowering biogenic methane target (24–47% below 2017 levels by 2050) and ruling out agricultural methane taxes. Commitment met.

Commitment: Reform the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee to ensure its functions, membership and mandate are appropriate.
Notes: NAWAC continues to operate but in October 2025 the associate agriculture minister announced pig welfare reforms that overrode NAWAC advice. Functions, membership and mandate of NAWAC itself not formally reformed.

Commitment: Cease implementation of new Significant Natural Areas and seek advice on the operation of existing Significant Natural Areas as part of the Government’s programme to reform the Resource Management Act.
Improve Farm Environment Plans so they are more cost-effective and pragmatic for farmers.
Enable farmers and landowners to offset sequestration against their on-farm emissions.
Notes: Existing ETS settings continue to allow forestry-based sequestration offsetting, but government exempted agriculture from ETS in June 2024. Framework for on-farm emissions offsetting has not been formally expanded per commitment.

Commitment: Replace the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020 to allow district councils more flexibility in how they meet environmental limits and seek advice on how to exempt councils from obligations under the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020 as soon aspracticable.
Notes: Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Act passed 24 October 2024, substantially amending NPS-FM 2020 (freshwater rules put on pause for farmers). Full replacement of NPS-FM not completed.

Commitment: Update the Crown Minerals Act 1991 to clarify its role as promoting the use of Crown minerals.
Notes: Crown Minerals Amendment Bill passed 31 July 2025 (after rare recommittal), clarifying Crown minerals regime to promote petroleum exploration. Commitment met.

Commitment: Explore the potential for a critical minerals list, where such minerals would have a preferential pathway for development once identified.
Notes: Government released a list of 35 critical minerals as part of its mining strategy on 16 September 2024; subsequent engagement with US on critical minerals supply (Feb 2026) and Tāiko Critical Minerals NZX debut (March 2026) shows the list is operational.

Commitment: Repeal the ban on offshore oil and gas exploration
Increase funding for the Department of Corrections to ensure there is sufficient prison capacity as required.
Invest in the construction of new youth justice beds.
Restore Three Strikes legislation, with amendments to tighten the definition of strike offences and ensure some benefit for pleading guilty.
Notes: Three Strikes Bill introduced 25 June 2024; Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill was about to become law in late March 2025, restoring tougher sentencing including three-strikes provisions.

Commitment: Abolish the previous Labour Government’s prisoner reduction target.
Take advice on amending the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009 so the threshold amount for seizing gang assets is $0 if an illegal firearm is found.
Strengthen the electronic monitoring regime.
Rewrite the Arms Act 1983 to provide for greater protection of public safety and simplify regulatory requirements to improve compliance and pass it through all stages during this term of Parliament.
Notes: Phase 4 of firearms reform programme (announced 14 June 2024) covers full rewrite of the Arms Act; Cabinet signed off on reforms 11 November 2025 but dropped semi-auto gun law changes, narrowing the rewrite scope. Rewrite not yet passed.

Commitment: Transfer responsibility for the Arms Act 1983, policy and regulation to the Ministry of Justice, and transfer the Firearms Safety Authority, administrator of the Act, to another department such as the Department of Internal Affairs.
Review whether the Firearms Registry is effectively improving public safety, beginning by June 2024.
Immediately begin to repeal and replace Part 6 of the Arms Act 1983 relating to clubs and ranges.
Reintroduce partnership schools and introduce a policy to allow state schools to become partnership (or charter) schools.
Explore further options to increase school choice and expand access to integrated and independent schools including reviewing the independent school funding formula to reflect student numbers.
Notes: Education and Training (System Reform) Amendment Bill passed third reading 24 June 2026, expanding school choice via charter pathways; independent school funding formula review may need separate action.

Commitment: Prioritise reporting and enforcement action to reduce truancy, including centrally collecting and publishing attendance data.
Improve the cost-effectiveness of the school lunch programme.
Replace the Fees Free programme with a final year fees free policy with no change before 2025.
Notes: Final-year fees free was delivered from 2025 after the coalition shifted Labour's first-year scheme; the policy was subsequently axed outright in Budget 2026 (effective 2027).

Commitment: Amend the Education and Training Act 2020 such that tertiary education providers receiving taxpayer funding must commit to a free speech policy.
Amend the Education and Training Act 2020 to enshrine educational attainment as the paramount objective for state schools.
Restore balance to the Aotearoa New Zealand’s Histories curriculum.
Notes: Curriculum redesign underway under System Reform Amendment Bill, but specific 'restoration of balance' to Aotearoa NZ Histories curriculum not visible.

Commitment: Broaden the terms of reference of the Royal Commission into the Covid-19 response, subject to public consultation.

Update Pharmac’s decision making model to ensure it appropriately takes patient voice into account and reform the funding model to account for positive fiscal impacts on the Crown of funding more medicines.
Notes: Independent Francis Review (Apr 2025) found Pharmac's approach 'not fit for purpose' and called for fundamental change in strategy and culture; Seymour accepted review, new CEO being recruited.

Commitment: Require the Ministry of Health to publish a Medicines Strategy every three years.
Better recognise people with overseas medical qualifications and experience for accreditation in NewZealand including consideration of an occupations tribunal.
Investigate build and lease-back arrangements for new hospitals.
Notes: New Public-Private Partnerships framework released Nov 2024 (with Labour backing); no specific build-and-lease-back hospitals delivered yet.

Commitment: Allow the sale of cold medication containing pseudoephedrine.
Allow appropriately qualified pharmacists to directly prescribe certain treatments.

Agree the terms of reference for the statutory requirement to review the End of Life Choice Act 2019 following consultation between the Parties, with any potential future changes to be progressed by way of a member’s bill, recognising this is a conscience issue.
Notes: MoH statutory review of End of Life Choice Act underway (Act required review by 2024); review report and any member's bill changes still pending.

Commitment: Examine the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme (MAPAS) and Otago equivalent to determine ifthey are delivering desired outcomes.
Notes: MAPAS/equivalent review assigned to Health Minister Reti (Dec 2023) but outcome of review not publicly reported.

Commitment: Introduce serious penalties for selling vapes to under 18s, and consider requiring a liquor licence to sell vapes.
Notes: Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill (No 2) passed under urgency Dec 2024: penalties for sales to under-18s lifted from $10k to $100k, plus disposable vape ban and visibility/proximity restrictions. Liquor-licence proposal not adopted.

Commitment: Implement sanctions, including electronic money management, for beneficiaries who can work but refuse to take agreed steps to find a job.
Develop an approved pool of doctors who can issue medical certificates to go onto a health and disability related benefit.
Remove Section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989.
Notes: Bill repealing Section 7AA passed third reading 3 Apr 2025 (68-54), awaiting Royal Assent.

Commitment: Create a truly independent monitoring and oversight agency for Oranga Tamariki.
Notes: Bill passed under urgency 26 Jun 2025: makes Independent Children's Monitor an Independent Crown Entity and reinstates a single Children's Commissioner.

Commitment: Improve the rights and responsibilities of caregivers to give them more autonomy.
Increase devolution of care decisions to relevant community organisations.

Immediately issue stop-work notices on several workstreams, including: Three Waters (with assets returned to council ownership), Auckland Light Rail, Let’s Get Wellington Moving, Income Insurance, Industry Transformation Plans, Lake Onslow Pumped Hydro.
Notes: ALR, LGWM, and Lake Onslow have been fully cancelled. Three Waters repeal has been announced.

Commitment: Amend the Public Service Act 2020 to clarify the role of the public service, drive performance, andensure accountability to deliver on the agenda of the government of the day.
Notes: Budget 2026 announces 8700-job public sector cut and agency mergers (~$2.4b savings), but no specific Public Service Act 2020 amendment identified.

Commitment: Ensure government contracts are awarded based on value, without racial discrimination.

Issue a Cabinet Office circular to all central government organisations that it is the Government’s expectation that public services should be prioritised on the basis of need, not race, within the first six months of Government.
Notes: Delivered several months late.

Commitment: Repeal the Canterbury Regional Council (Ngāi Tahu Representation) Act 2022.
Pass the Constitution (Enabling a 4-Year Term) Amendment Bill through first reading in the first 15 months of the term.
Notes: Constitution (Enabling a 4-Year Term) Amendment Bill introduced 27 Feb 2025 (within the 15-month deadline) and debated at first reading in March 2025; Justice Select Committee reported back, awaiting second reading.

Commitment: Introduce a Treaty Principles Bill based on existing ACT policy and support it to a Select Committeeas soon as practicable.
Notes: Treaty Principles Bill select committee process ran Jan-Sep 2025 (300k+ submissions). Select committee recommended bill not proceed; Government now pursuing 19 targeted Treaty clause amendments instead. No third reading.

Commitment: Meet with councils and communities to establish regional requirements for recovery from Cyclone Gabrielle and other recent major flooding events.
Make any additional Orders in Council needed to speed up cyclone and flood recovery efforts.
Introduce legislation to remove the Auckland Fuel Tax.
Cancel fuel tax hikes.
Notes: Fuel tax hikes may still take effect after the next election.

Commitment: Introduce legislation to ban gang patches, stop gang members gathering in public, and stop known gang offenders from communicating with one another.
Notes: Legislation introduced

Commitment: Give police greater powers to search gang members for firearms and make gang membership an aggravating factor at sentencing.
Notes: Legislation introduced

Commitment: Stop taxpayer funding for Section 27 cultural reports.
Introduce legislation to extend eligibility to offence-based rehabilitation programmes to remand prisoners.
Begin work to crack down on serious youth offending.
Enable more virtual participation in court proceedings.
Introduce legislation to repeal the Water Services Entities Act 2022 (Three Waters).
Improve security for the health workforce in hospital emergency departments.
Redesign the English and maths curricula for primary school students.
Begin disestablishing Te Pukenga.
Set five major targets for health system, including for wait times and cancer treatment.
Extend free breast cancer screening to those aged up to 74.
Establish a priority one category on the social housing waitlist to move families out of emergency housing into permanent homes more quickly.
Commission an independent review into Kāinga Ora’s financial situation, procurement, and asset management.
